verdict_rationale.summary: V5 pressure-gradient-dependent drainage simulation reveals that the eShunt may not have a significant over-drainage problem. The over-drainage literature (65 Scopus results for 'shunt overdrainage siphon') establishes that over-drainage is caused by the SIPHON EFFECT in VP shunts (long peritoneal catheter creating hydrostatic column). The eShunt drains from the subarachnoid space to the dural venous sinus — both in the head, with minimal hydrostatic column (engineering blueprint confirms 3-5 mmHg differential). Without the siphon effect, the eShunt's pressure-gradient-dependent drainage is self-limiting: the one-way valve closes when ICP drops to P_venous + P_valve = 2 + 5 = 7 mmHg, preventing ICP from reaching the over-drainage threshold (5 mmHg). The adaptive drainage controller (M5/SC3/hybrid) solves a problem that the physics says may not exist for the eShunt. This is an Article XX problem-existence failure — the same type of finding that killed #7 (M5 flexible neck solved a hypothetical venous trauma problem).
verdict_rationale.v4_0pct_was_not_a_bug: The 0% over-drainage in V4 and V5 is not a coding bug, not a modeling error, and not an artifact. It is the model correctly telling us that the eShunt's drainage geometry prevents over-drainage. The valve closes before ICP reaches the over-drainage threshold.

q1_does_failure_occur.v4_answer: YES — over-drainage is documented in CSF shunts (10-20%)
q1_does_failure_occur.v5_revised_answer: UNCERTAIN FOR ESHUNT — over-drainage is documented for VP SHUNTS (siphon effect). The eShunt's short drainage path (subarachnoid to venous sinus, co-located in head, 3-5 mmHg differential per engineering blueprint) may not produce the siphon effect that causes VP shunt over-drainage. Scopus search 'shunt overdrainage siphon' returns 65 results — ALL focus on anti-siphon devices for VP/peritoneal shunts. No eShunt-specific over-drainage data found.
q1_does_failure_occur.verdict: FAIL — problem existence not established for eShunt specifically

q2_does_it_matter_to_buyer.v5_revised_answer: CONDITIONAL — matters only IF eShunt over-drains. If the eShunt geometry inherently prevents over-drainage, the adaptive controller is unnecessary.
q2_does_it_matter_to_buyer.verdict: CONDITIONAL FAIL — buyer value depends on problem existence

article_xx_re_assessment.q3_does_mechanism_change_physical_quanti: YES — controllers modulate drainage rate. This is not the failure point.
article_xx_re_assessment.q4_is_change_large_enough: CANNOT ASSESS — if over-drainage doesn't occur, the reduction is of a zero quantity (same as #7).
article_xx_re_assessment.q5_does_intervention_create_larger_failu: YES — adaptive controller introduces under-drainage risk (ICP elevation), sensor failure modes, and controller oscillation. These risks are NOT justified if the over-drainage problem doesn't exist.
article_xx_re_assessment.gate_verdict: FAIL — Article XX problem-existence gate fails for the eShunt specifically. The over-drainage problem is documented for VP shunts but not for the eShunt's venous-sinus drainage geometry.

prior_art_evidence.scopus_search: shunt overdrainage siphon → 65 results. All focus on anti-siphon devices for VP/peritoneal shunts.
prior_art_evidence.key_finding: Over-drainage is caused by the siphon effect (hydrostatic column in long peritoneal catheters). Anti-siphon devices (gravitational valves, flow-regulating valves) are the standard solution. The eShunt's short drainage path (subarachnoid to venous sinus) does not create a significant hydrostatic column.
prior_art_evidence.eshunt_engineering_blueprint: eShunt operates at 3-5 mmHg differential, flow path: subarachnoid → eShunt → one-way valve → dural venous sinus. No peritoneal catheter, no long hydrostatic column.

what_would_overturn_this_verdict.if_clinical_data_shows_eshunt_over_drain: If post-market surveillance of the eShunt documents over-drainage complications, the problem exists and the adaptive controller is justified. This requires clinical data, not simulation.
what_would_overturn_this_verdict.if_the_eshunt_valve_is_set_below_3_mmhg: If the eShunt valve opening pressure is set very low (< 3 mmHg), over-drainage could occur even without the siphon effect. Need to verify the actual clinical valve setting.
what_would_overturn_this_verdict.if_there_is_a_hydrostatic_column_not_mod: If the eShunt is deployed in the jugular vein (not the dural venous sinus), there may be a hydrostatic column from the CSF space to the jugular vein that creates a siphon effect. Need to verify the actual deployment site.

branch_disposition.frozen_reason: Article XX problem-existence gate fails. Over-drainage is documented for VP shunts (siphon effect) but not for the eShunt (short drainage path, no hydrostatic column, 3-5 mmHg differential). The adaptive drainage controller (M5/SC3/hybrid) solves a problem that the physics says may not exist for the eShunt. Same failure type as #7 (M5 flexible neck solved a hypothetical venous trauma problem).
branch_disposition.v_next_rationale: The negative ceiling is at the PROBLEM-EXISTENCE level (does over-drainage occur in the eShunt?). This can only be overturned by clinical data, not by mechanism development. No V6 simulation can create a problem that the physics says doesn't exist.

impact_on_portfolio.active_frontier: #6 (mechanism reset) + #9 + #10 + replacement candidates (RC1, RC3, RC4, RC5, RC8, RC9)
impact_on_portfolio.lesson: The eShunt's drainage geometry (subarachnoid to venous sinus, short path, no hydrostatic column) is fundamentally different from VP shunts (long peritoneal catheter, siphon effect). Problems documented for VP shunts (over-drainage, siphon) may NOT apply to the eShunt. Always verify the problem exists for the SPECIFIC device geometry, not just for the general device class. This is the second Article XX problem-existence failure (#7 was the first).
